why: Engineers need answers that always come from the current approved version of each standard, and the biggest value is linking answers to road asset data, which needs Azure.
knowledge: Council road and transport policies (Word / PDF), current and superseded versions.
Engineering standards and technical specifications, with their version history.
Standard drawings and design guidelines used for road works.
Asset data from the council's road asset register (road hierarchy, pavement and signage records).

technical: Move the prototype into an Azure DevOps repo and rebuild the front end in Vue and Bootstrap, hosted on Azure App Service with council (Entra ID) sign-in.
Move all AI calls into an Azure Function App, with Claude through Microsoft Foundry or the council's Anthropic agreement. Keys live in Key Vault, never in the page.
Load each standard into an Azure AI Search index split by clause, with document, version and effective date, so answers quote the clause and version they used.
Keep superseded versions in the index, flagged as superseded, so the version comparison works but answers default to the current version.
Read road asset details from the council's road asset register (through Boomi or Logic Apps) so a road lookup shows its recorded widths, lighting and drainage next to the standard that applies.
Keep the road check rules (which asset field is checked against which clause and value) in a table the standard owners can review, and re-run them whenever a new version of a standard is loaded.
Strip or pseudonymise personal information before anything goes to the model.
Security review against the OWASP Top 10 and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps (including prompt injection hidden in document text).
Dev, Test and Prod resource groups, Application Insights logging, cost alerts and CI/CD pipelines in Azure DevOps.
Model access: a Claude deployment in Microsoft Foundry or an enterprise Anthropic API key (needs an ICT-DA exception as it's outside the listed stack).
business: Confirm the business owner (Transport Planning and Assets), scope and success measures, and raise an Azure DevOps card (why and how).
Agree who owns each standard and how a new version gets approved and loaded.
Agree with asset and standard owners how road check results are used: a road below the current standard is not a defect on its own, and the current version applies to new work, upgrades and renewals.
Build a test plan and an AI evaluation set (real engineering questions with the expected clause and version), then run UAT with engineers.
Make it clear answers are guidance: engineers check the clause before relying on it for design decisions.
Train engineers and set up support: who to ask and how to report a wrong or out-of-date answer.
Get ICT-DA, CAB, PGG and Business System Owner approval, with a Go Live plan, service transition document and support playbook.

technical: Set it up as a Claude Project for Transport Planning and Assets in the council's enterprise Claude, with the prototype's instructions as the project instructions.
Connect the SharePoint library that holds the standards so answers use the current published versions.
Tell it to quote the document, clause and version for every answer, and say plainly when the standards don't cover the question.
Admin settings checked: data retention, sharing and connector permissions.
business: Confirm the business owner, who will use it and what it must never do (it explains standards, engineers make the decisions).
Keep only approved standards in the library, with superseded versions clearly labelled.
Test it with 20 to 30 real engineering questions and record how often it cites the right clause and version.
Pilot with a small group of engineers, give them a 30-minute walkthrough, and collect feedback for two to four weeks.
Enterprise Claude seats for the engineers who will use it.
No link to the road asset register, so engineers look up asset details themselves and the road check tab is not available.
Get the use case approved (ICT-DA and PGG) and confirm privacy settings before rolling it out wider.

Owns the process, agrees what good looks like and signs off going live.
Keep the documents the tool relies on current and approved.
Builds the solution, runs testing and hands over to support.
